title: \(\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\) versus MA
formal:
Do the following two classes of ordinary decision languages coincide?
\[\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm{MA}.\]
An \(\mathrm{MA}\) language has a polynomial-length classical witness and a polynomial-time randomized verifier: a yes-instance has some witness accepted with probability at least \(2/3\), and every witness to a no-instance is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\).

For \(\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\), the witness predicate must additionally be an ordinary BPP language on pairs. Its acceptance probability is therefore always at most \(1/3\) or at least \(2/3\), including for every unsuccessful witness on a yes-instance. The equality asks whether every MA language admits some verifier with that stronger all-pairs gap, possibly with a different witness encoding and polynomial length bound.
why: Existential witnesses and randomized verification interact differently depending on whether every witness must induce a valid bounded-error decision. Resolving this equality would determine whether the additional gap requirement changes computational power or only the presentation of a verifier. The distinction is fundamental when probabilistic predicates are nested beneath quantifiers in classical and quantum complexity hierarchies.

sentences: The question asks whether existential quantification over an ordinary BPP language has exactly the power of Merlin–Arthur verification.
Both settings use a polynomial-size witness chosen before a uniform randomized polynomial-time check.
Existential BPP additionally requires a bounded-error gap for every input-witness pair, even for unsuccessful witnesses on yes-instances.
Equality permits changing the verifier, so one verifier with intermediate probabilities is not a counterexample.
An oracle separation is known, while the ordinary class equality remains the source’s unresolved target.

definitions:
A language is a subset of \(\{0,1\}^*\). Use uniform finite-program probabilistic multitape Turing machines, with independent fair random bits, binary input and an accept/reject output. Every random-bit sequence must lead to a halt in time polynomial in input length. Bit operations, random-bit generation and input and output handling count as work. No advice, oracle or quantum register is supplied.

For definiteness, encode a pair by \(\langle x,y\rangle=1^{|x|}0xy\). The initial unary field specifies exactly how many subsequent bits form \(x\), and the rest form \(y\). Strings without such a complete parse are malformed; a pair verifier rejects them deterministically. This is a uniquely decodable, polynomial-size encoding. On well-formed pairs, the time bound is at most \(C(|x|+|y|+2)^d\) for fixed positive integers \(C,d\), and the usual polynomial bound applies to all encoded inputs. Let \(a_V(x,y)=\Pr[V(\langle x,y\rangle)=1]\).

The class \(\mathrm{MA}\) consists of languages \(L\) for which there are a verifier \(V\) as above and fixed positive integers \(c,k\), giving a witness bound \(p(n)=c(n+1)^k\), such that
\[x\in L\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists y,\ |y|\le p(|x|)\ \text{and}\ a_V(x,y)\ge2/3,\]
\[x\notin L\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall y,\ |y|\le p(|x|)\ \Longrightarrow\ a_V(x,y)\le1/3.\]
The witness is chosen before the verifier's random bits are drawn, so it cannot depend on their realized values. When \(x\in L\), the probabilities for other witnesses may be anywhere in \([0,1]\). The language is total as a decision problem: every input is either in \(L\) or in its complement; this is not a promise-MA problem with unclassified inputs.

A language \(A\) is in \(\mathrm{BPP}\) if some uniform randomized polynomial-time machine accepts each \(z\in A\) with probability at least \(2/3\) and each \(z\notin A\) with probability at most \(1/3\). In particular, every input has the required gap. Define the existential operator by
\[L\in\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists A\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \exists c,k\ge1\ \forall x,\quad x\in L\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \exists y\ \bigl(|y|\le c(|x|+1)^k\ \land\ \langle x,y\rangle\in A\bigr).\]
Here \(c,k\) are integers. The set \(A\) may be assumed to reject malformed pair encodings. The witness bound is a polynomial size bound, not a bound on the cost of finding the witness.

Equivalently, \(L\) has an MA verifier \(W\) that also satisfies
\[\forall x,y\in\{0,1\}^*,\qquad a_W(x,y)\in[0,1/3]\cup[2/3,1].\]
This condition includes witnesses exceeding the chosen length bound; they may be rejected deterministically. It requires one uniform verifier for all \(x,y\), not a separately chosen randomized algorithm for each fixed witness. There is no requirement that a new \(W\) preserve the original verifier's probabilities or use its witness bound.

It follows from these definitions that \(\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{MA}\). Thus the substantive equality direction is that every language in MA has some globally gapped witness predicate. A negative answer is a language in MA with no such predicate under any polynomial witness bound. Merely presenting one MA verifier with a probability in the gap does not establish that its language lacks a different globally gapped verifier.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the equality in the uniform, unrelativized language setting. A proof must establish a globally bounded-error witness predicate for every MA language, including exact polynomial runtime and witness-length guarantees. It may change the verifier and witness encoding and need not give an effective conversion between arbitrary machine descriptions. A refutation must prove that some MA language has no existential-BPP representation under any allowed verifier and polynomial bound. One verifier with intermediate acceptance probabilities, or an oracle separation, does not by itself refute the ordinary class equality.

context_blocks.text: Definition 16 applies the existential operator to ordinary languages. Remark 17 explains why fixing a witness in an MA verifier need not leave a BPP computation: a nonwinning witness on a yes-instance may lie inside the error gap. This does not itself prove that the language has no other suitable verifier.

The source encounters this distinction when bounding quantum hierarchies with classical witnesses. Its stronger-oracle simulations handle a different resource class; they do not establish the desired ordinary BPP predicate.

Fenner, Fortnow, Kurtz and Li construct an oracle relative to which MA is not contained even in nondeterministic polynomial time with access to a BPP oracle. Since existential BPP is contained in that latter class, the two target classes can differ relative to a common oracle. This is an obstruction to a proof valid under every oracle, not an unconditional separation.
